content: Pediatric Basic Life Support (BLS) refers to life-saving interventions for children, including high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and rescue breaths, often supplemented by the use of an Automated External Defibrillator (AED). Importance of Bystander CPR Bystander CPR plays a critical role in improving survival outcomes for children experiencing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Research by Maryam Y. Naim et al. demonstrated that communities practicing bystander CPR had better survival rates in children under 18 years of age. Studies involving 781 children revealed that approximately half of all cardio-respiratory arrests in children under 12 months occur outside the hospital. Favorable prognostic factors upon arrival at the emergency department include a short interval between arrest and hospital arrival, resuscitation lasting less than 20 minutes, and the administration of fewer than two doses of epinephrine. Classification of Pediatric BLS Pediatric BLS is categorized by age: Infants: Less than 1 year old. Children: 1 year to puberty. Adults: Post-puberty. BLS is further classified based on the setting: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (IHCA) Causes of Cardiac Arrest in Children Common causes of cardiac arrest in children include: Ventricular fibrillation. Pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Pre-existing cardiac disorders such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, anomalous coronary artery, long QT syndrome, and myocarditis. Drug intoxication (e.g., tricyclic antidepressants, digoxin, cocaine). Commotio cordis (blunt chest trauma). Goals of Resuscitation The primary goal of resuscitation is to deliver high-quality CPR to improve survival and neurological outcomes. High-quality CPR involves: Rate: 100-120 chest compressions per minute. Depth: 4 cm for infants and 5 cm for children older than 1 year. Chest Recoil: Allow full chest recoil to facilitate blood flow back to the heart. Rescue Breaths: CPR with rescue breaths is associated with better neurological outcomes compared to compression-only CPR, especially in children over 1 year of age. Approach to Suspected Cardiac or Respiratory Arrest 1. Ensure the safety of the rescuer and the child. 2. Call for help and activate emergency medical services (EMS). Retrieve an AED if available. 3. Check for responsiveness and breathing. If the child is not breathing or gasping, start CPR. 4. Check for a pulse (brachial pulse in infants, femoral or brachial pulse in children over 1 year) for no more than 10 seconds. 5. Follow the C-A-B sequence (Compression, Airway, Breathing) as per updated guidelines. CPR Techniques For a single rescuer: Perform 30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths. For two rescuers: Perform 15 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths, alternating roles every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue. Use the head-tilt and chin-lift method to open the airway. For suspected spinal trauma, use the jaw-thrust maneuver without head tilt. Use of AED Place the AED pads appropriately: one below the right clavicle and the other on the left chest lateral to the breast. Follow AED prompts, stopping CPR only when the AED is analyzing or delivering a shock. Resume compressions immediately after the shock, minimizing interruptions. Foreign Body Airway Obstruction (FBAO) For mild obstruction: Monitor the child and allow them to clear the airway. For severe obstruction: Perform the Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts) for children or back blows and chest compressions for infants. If the child becomes unresponsive, start CPR immediately. After 30 compressions, check the airway for visible obstructions and remove them if accessible. Special Circumstances Tracheostomy: Provide rescue breaths through the tracheostomy tube. If ineffective, suction the tube or use bag-mask ventilation. Spinal Trauma: Avoid cervical spine movement. Use the jaw-thrust maneuver for ventilation. Elevate the back in children under 7 years to achieve a neutral position. Drowning: Begin CPR as soon as the child is removed from the water. If trained, initiate in-water ventilation while immobilizing the spine if trauma is suspected. General Considerations Performing high-quality CPR according to these guidelines can save lives and improve neurological outcomes. Communities should be encouraged to undergo BLS training to ensure prompt and effective intervention during emergencies. However, more pediatric-specific clinical studies are needed to refine guidelines further, particularly regarding compression depth and outcomes in younger children.
